# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
# Critical reading of the Varga and Holm re-examination of Halden

This comment does real work. Using the Halden microdata, it puts numbers on several problems that could only be suspected from the working paper: the scheduled-hours denominator, manager-rated output, the nominal revenue figure, and selective attrition. Its attrition finding is a serious charge against Halden, not a minor correction.

But its headline conclusion, that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact", is not supported by its own analysis. It also contradicts the randomised evidence the comment itself cites.

## What holds up

### The arithmetic is almost all correct

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Actual hours, 27 organisations | 40.3 → 34.6 = −14.1%; ratio 0.859 |
| Actual hours, 17 organisations | 40.4 → 34.8 = −13.9%; ratio 0.861 |
| Table 2, row 2 | 95.1 / 0.800 = +18.9% |
| Table 2, row 3 | 98.4 / 0.859 = +14.6% |
| Table 2, row 4 | 95.4 / 0.861 = +10.8% |
| Real revenue | 1.014 / 1.041 = −2.6% |

### The attrition finding is the most important new fact

If the microdata are right, Halden described the withdrawals inaccurately. Seven of the nine organisations left *after* the schedule began, and most cited inability to keep up output. That is post-treatment attrition of the least successful cases, and the working paper presented it as harmless pre-pilot dropout. Halden's authors should respond to this directly.

### The per-hour and revenue points are correct and now quantified

The point that any output index above 80 registers as a per-hour gain was already clear from Halden's own tables. The comment adds hard figures: actual hours fell by about 14% rather than 20%, and revenue fell by about 2.6% in real terms.

## Problems in the comment

### 1. The hours breakdown doesn't add up

The comment explains the smaller fall in hours by longer days (+0.7 hours per day) and work on the day off (1.6 hours per week). Applied to a 32-hour schedule, that gives 32 + (4 × 0.7) + 1.6 = **36.4 hours**, not the reported **34.6**. Measured from baseline days of about 8.06 hours, the total is higher still, about 36.6.

That leaves roughly two hours unexplained. Either some components are averaged across different sets of organisations, or one of the figures is wrong. This doesn't affect Table 2, which uses the 34.6 total, but it needs reconciling.

### 2. "Record-based" output is not automatically the true figure

The comment treats submitted records as ground truth and the manager index as biased. Two problems:

- **Some records measure time, not output.** "Billable hours delivered" fall almost automatically when hours fall. Using them as output pushes the per-hour gain toward zero by construction. The comment doesn't say how many of the 23 organisations used billable hours. That matters most for professional services, Halden's largest sector.
- **Records can be incomplete.** Single metrics like tickets closed or units produced may leave out output a manager reasonably counted.

Managers exceeding the records in 19 of 23 cases does suggest optimism. But the 3.8-point gap is an upper bound on manager bias, not a clean measure of it.

### 3. The abstract says attrition was corrected, but it wasn't

The abstract says "correcting the first three" problems, which include attrition, brings the gain down to 10.8%. Table 2 only corrects output and hours, within subsets of the 61 *survivors*.

Attrition is described but never quantified. A bounding exercise was possible: assume the nine leavers had, say, no per-hour gain or a fall in output, and show how the estimate moves.

### 4. The novelty argument is the weakest part, and the comment leaves the obvious test unrun

- **It extrapolates two survey points.** It draws a straight line through 0.61 SD at month three and 0.29 SD at month six to predict a return to baseline at month ten. That assumes the decline is linear, and two points cannot show that.
- **Energy is not output.** A self-reported energy score is a different measure from productivity.
- **The direct test was available.** The microdata contain *monthly* output indices, and time-tracking data exist for 27 organisations. If output per hour declined from month one to month six, the comment could have shown it. It doesn't report this.
- **It shifts the burden of proof.** Saying the burden lies with those claiming a durable effect is fine as caution. It does not support a positive claim that the effect is zero.

### 5. The conclusion goes beyond the comment's own data

The analysis ends with an estimated gain of about **+10.8%** remaining after correction. The data note correctly says this describes non-random subsets. Yet the conclusion says the gains are "entirely an artifact", and extends that to reduced-hours schemes in general. That is not consistent with:

- the comment's own remaining estimate of about 11%;
- its own caveat that subset results do not describe the whole pilot;
- the abstract's more careful wording, that the problems "account for most" of the gain.

Cutting 23.4% to 10.8% is a reduction of a little over half. It is not elimination.

### 6. It uses the Varden trial selectively

The comment calls Varden's counter stratum "the most reliable finding in the literature." It does not mention Varden's **case-processing** stratum, which:

- comes from the same randomised trial;
- is larger, with 14 offices against 10, and has a tighter confidence interval;
- uses administrative output and actual hours from timesheets, exactly the corrections the comment recommends;
- found **+12.5%** output per actual hour, with a 95% CI of +6.9% to +18.4%, at nine months, against a concurrent control.

That result is very close to the comment's own corrected 10.8%. Two independent methods give similar answers in non-coverage work, and the comment cites the trial only for the stratum that supports its conclusion. Novelty can't be ruled out in Varden either, since treated staff knew their assignment. But nine months is already beyond the month-six window the comment treats as suspect.

### 7. It holds the two explanations to different standards

The comment dismisses Varden's meetings analysis as a post hoc subgroup story. That is fair as far as it goes, but Varden's authors had already said all of this themselves:

- the analysis was not registered;
- it rests on seven offices;
- it "cannot establish a mechanism";
- a confirmatory test is registered for 24 months.

They did not claim it as a mechanism, so the comment is arguing against a position Varden didn't take.

Meanwhile, the comment's own novelty explanation is just as post hoc. It rests on two points of a self-reported scale and is offered with more confidence. Both explanations should be treated as hypotheses.

### 8. Smaller points

- **Retail.** The 11.2% fall in retail output from records rests on three organisations.
- **Exit reasons.** Six withdrawals cited workload and two cited scheduling, which leaves one unaccounted for.
- **Deflator.** CPI is a reasonable but rough deflator for business revenue. Output prices in these sectors may have moved differently, though the direction of the correction is surely right.
- **Wellbeing results.** The comment says nothing about sickness absence. Varden's randomised trial found a 29% fall, so "the best-supported finding is the negative one" leaves out a positive finding that is well supported.

## Where the three documents leave things

| Question | Best current evidence |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain against scheduled hours | Overstated. Roughly halved once actual hours and records are used (Varga and Holm; Varden). |
| Per-hour gain in non-coverage work | About +11–13% per actual hour, found independently in Halden's corrected subsets and Varden's randomised case-processing stratum. Not shown to be zero. |
| Output per employee in non-coverage work | Small loss, around −2% to −5%, with a CI that allows up to about −7%. |
| Coverage-bound work | Output per employee falls by about 7–11% and service worsens. Consistent across all three documents. |
| Sector-general claim | Not supported. |
| Durability | Unknown. Novelty is plausible but untested. Halden's monthly data and Varden's 24-month follow-up can test it. |
| Mechanism (rest, meetings or novelty) | Unresolved. All three explanations are hypotheses. |
| Sickness absence | Reduced, and the effect survives randomisation. |
| Halden's reporting of withdrawals | Apparently inaccurate. Halden's authors should respond. |

In short, Varga and Holm convincingly show that Halden's 23.4% was inflated. They do not show that the true figure is zero, and the best evidence available, including evidence they cite, points to a modest real per-hour gain in non-coverage work.
